A river begins as rain or melting snow high in the hills. Small streams join together as they flow downhill, and the water slowly carves a valley into the land. Along the way, the river carries sand, mud and small stones, which settle wherever the current slows down. Farmers have long settled near rivers because the soil there is rich and water is easy to reach. Towns grew at places where people could cross the river safely, and many of those crossings later became bridges and busy markets. Today rivers still supply drinking water, move goods by boat and produce electricity, but they also need care. When forests are cut or waste is dumped into the water, fish disappear and floods become more dangerous. Protecting a river means looking after the whole area that drains into it, from the hills to the sea.
